If same-arm switching-layer occupation is excluded, only the two opposite-context modes remain and (15) forces \(v=1-u\), producing \((u_0,b_0)\).  But (11) and the continuum in (18)--(21) show that this exclusion is not a consequence of the exact recursion or of the differential-inclusion theorem: same-arm modes survive throughout the shrinking switching layer.  The graph is discontinuous there, and the preceding argument supplies neither an avoidance estimate for switching-surface convergence nor a quantitative hitting, escape, or equicontinuity estimate uniform over compact initial sets.  It therefore establishes neither finite almost-sure tail selection nor zero switching-surface probability, and it does not establish compact-uniform moduli \(r_T(K_0),\delta_T(K_0)\).  Since membership in \(\mathfrak P_T\) requires precisely such tail-selection and uniform-attraction properties, no membership or inference conclusion is asserted.  This proves all parts of the theorem.

statements.statement:
Let \(p\in[1,\infty)\), \(\gamma>0\), and let \((X_i,\mathcal G_i)_{i=1}^n\) be a scalar martingale-difference sequence with \(n\ge2\) and \(\max_i\|X_i\|_\infty\le\gamma\). Put \(s^2=\sum_{i=1}^nE[X_i^2]\), \(V^2=s^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^nE[X_i^2\mid\mathcal G_{i-1}]\), and \(D=\sup_x|P\{s^{-1}\sum_iX_i\le x\}-\Phi(x)|\). There is a constant \(C_{p,\gamma}\) such that
\[
D\le C_{p,\gamma}\left\{\frac{n\log n}{s^3}+\left(\|V^2-1\|_p^p+s^{-2p}\right)^{1/(2p+1)}\right\}.
\]

statements.statement: For Saco's logged-propensity, predictably scored martingale AIPW/DML estimator at a prespecified horizon, the realized-quadratic-variation score statistic and its feasible Studentized version converge pointwise to \(N(0,1)\), and the associated Wald interval has asymptotically correct coverage without a deterministic variance-stabilization assumption.

source.verbatim_statement: Theorem 5.14 (Studentized fixed-horizon inference without variance stabilization). Under the listed assumptions, S_T/sqrt(Q_T) converges in distribution to N(0,1), and the practical Studentized statistic sqrt(n_eff)(theta_hat-theta_0)/V_hat^{1/2} converges in distribution to N(0,1). Consequently, the Wald interval (4.7) has asymptotically correct coverage at the prespecified horizon, without requiring variance stabilization.

statements.statement:
Let \((X_{T,t},\mathcal G_{T,t})_{t=1}^T\) be a scalar martingale-difference triangular array under \(P\), let \(0\le k_T<T\), and suppose \(|X_{T,t}|\le L<\infty\) almost surely. Let \(\lambda_T\) be \(\mathcal G_{T,k_T}\)-measurable and satisfy \(0<v_-\le\lambda_T\le v_+<\infty\) almost surely. If
\[
 \Delta_T:=E_P\left|T^{-1}\sum_{t=k_T+1}^T
 E_P[X_{T,t}^2\mid\mathcal G_{T,t-1}]-\lambda_T\right|\longrightarrow0,
\]
then
\[
 \sup_{z\in\mathbb R}\left|P\left\{T^{-1/2}\sum_{t=k_T+1}^T X_{T,t}\le z\right\}
 -E_P\Phi\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt{\lambda_T}}\right)\right|\longrightarrow0.
\]
The conclusion is uniform over any collection of arrays having common \(L,v_-,v_+\) and a common upper bound on \(\Delta_T\) that tends to zero.
statements.proof_tex:
Put
\[
 Q_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=k_T+1}^T
 E_P[X_{T,t}^2\mid\mathcal G_{T,t-1}].
\tag{1}
\]
Fix \(\eta>0\) and partition \([v_-,v_+]\) into finitely many Borel intervals \(I_r\) of diameter at most \(\eta\).  The events \(B_r=\{\lambda_T\in I_r\}\) belong to \(\mathcal G_{T,k_T}\); choose \(\lambda_r\in I_r\).  For each cell of positive probability let \(P_r=P(\,\cdot\mid B_r)\).  Since \(B_r\in\mathcal G_{T,k_T}\subseteq\mathcal G_{T,t-1}\) for \(t>k_T\), testing against bounded \(\mathcal G_{T,t-1}\)-measurable functions gives
\[
 E_{P_r}[X_{T,t}\mid\mathcal G_{T,t-1}]=0
 \quad\text{on }B_r.
\tag{2}
\]
Thus the suffix remains a martingale-difference array under \(P_r\).

Define
\[
 d_r=E_{P_r}|Q_T-\lambda_T|+\eta,qquad
 q_r=E_{P_r}Q_T,qquad s_r^2=Tq_r.
\tag{3}
\]
Since \(|\lambda_T-\lambda_r|\le\eta\) on \(B_r\),
\[
 |q_r-\lambda_r|\le d_r,qquad
 \sum_rP(B_r)d_r\le\Delta_T+\eta.
\tag{4}
\]
Call a cell good when \(d_r\le v_-/2\).  Markov's inequality for the weighted sum in (4) bounds the total mass of bad cells by \(2(\Delta_T+\eta)/v_-\).  On a good cell, \(q_r\ge v_-/2\), and the normalized predictable quadratic variation in the cited Mourrat bound is \(V_r^2=Q_T/q_r\).  Moreover,
\[
 E_{P_r}|Q_T-q_r|
 \le2E_{P_r}|Q_T-\lambda_T|+2\eta\le2d_r,
 \qquad E_{P_r}|V_r^2-1|\le\frac{4d_r}{v_-}.
\tag{5}
\]
For all sufficiently large \(T\), the suffix contains at least two increments.  Otherwise boundedness would give \(Q_T\le L^2/T\), contradicting \(\Delta_T\to0\) and \(\lambda_T\ge v_-\).  Its number of increments is at most \(T\), and \(s_r^2\ge Tv_-/2\).  Applying \(\mathrm{lem:mourrat\text{-}bounded\text{-}martingale\text{-}clt}\) with \(p=1\) under \(P_r\) yields a constant depending only on \(L,v_-,v_+\) such that
\[
 \sup_z\left|P_r\!\left\{T^{-1/2}\sum_{t>k_T}X_{T,t}\le z\right\}
 -\Phi\!\left(\frac z{\sqrt{q_r}}\right)\right|
 \le C\left\{\frac{\log T}{\sqrt T}+(d_r+T^{-1})^{1/3}\right\}.
\tag{6}
\]
For \(q\ge v_-/2\), differentiation gives
\[
 \sup_z\left|\frac{\partial}{\partial q}
 \Phi\!\left(\frac z{\sqrt q}\right)\right|
 =\sup_u\frac{|u|\phi(u)}{2q}\le C_{v_-}.
\tag{7}
\]
Therefore, on every good cell, (3)--(5) and (7) imply
\[
 \sup_z\left|\Phi\!\left(\frac z{\sqrt{q_r}}\right)
 -E_{P_r}\Phi\!\left(\frac z{\sqrt{\lambda_T}}\right)\right|
 \le C_{v_-}d_r.
\tag{8}
\]
Multiply (6) and (8) by \(P(B_r)\), sum over cells, bound each bad-cell discrepancy by one, and use concavity of \(x^{1/3}\).  Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\sup_z\left|P\!\left\{T^{-1/2}\sum_{t>k_T}X_{T,t}\le z\right\}
 -E_P\Phi\!\left(\frac z{\sqrt{\lambda_T}}\right)\right|\\
 &\quad\le C\left\{\frac{\log T}{\sqrt T}
 +(\Delta_T+\eta+T^{-1})^{1/3}+\Delta_T+\eta\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]
Taking \(\eta=T^{-1}\) proves the assertion.  Every constant in (9) depends only on the common \(L,v_-,v_+\), proving uniformity.
statements.justification: This conditioning-free finite-partition lemma is the glue that turns an early-measurable variance proxy into a marginal Gaussian-mixture approximation.
statements.gap: Mourrat supplies the quantitative deterministic-variance martingale bound; the finite-partition adaptation to a random early-measurable variance is derived here.
statements.consumer: Theorem 1 uses the lemma to obtain the strongest label-free law allowed by the attraction primitives.

statements.statement: Let \(F:\mathbb R^r\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^r\) have closed graph, nonempty compact convex values, and linear growth. In the terminology of Bena\"im, Hofbauer, and Sorin, every bounded perturbed solution of \(\dot x\in F(x)\) is an asymptotic pseudotrajectory, and its limit set is internally chain transitive.

Theorem 3.6: Let y be a bounded perturbed solution to (I). Then the limit set of y is internally chain transitive. Theorem 4.2: Any bounded solution y of (II) is an APT of (I).

statements.statement: Let \(0<a\le b<\infty\), and let \((U_n)\) be random symmetric \(d\)-by-\(d\) matrices satisfying \(aI_d\preceq U_n\preceq bI_d\) almost surely. There are a subsequence \((n_k)\) and a Borel probability measure \(\mu\), supported on \(\mathcal K_{a,b}=\{u=u^\top:aI_d\preceq u\preceq bI_d\}\), such that \(E[f(U_{n_k})]\to\int f(u)\,d\mu(u)\) for every continuous \(f:\mathcal K_{a,b}\to\mathbb R\).
statements.proof_tex:
Identify a symmetric \(d\)-by-\(d\) matrix with its \(s=d(d+1)/2\) upper-triangular entries.  The set
\[
 \mathcal K_{a,b}=\{u=u^\top:aI_d\preceq u\preceq bI_d\}
\]
is closed and bounded in \(\mathbb R^s\), hence compact.  For every integer \(r\ge1\), choose a finite Borel partition \(\mathcal P_r\) of \(\mathcal K_{a,b}\) into cells of diameter at most \(2^{-r}\), with \(\mathcal P_{r+1}\) refining \(\mathcal P_r\).  Such partitions follow by intersecting each old cell with a finite ball cover and disjointifying in a fixed order.

There are countably many cells in \(\bigcup_r\mathcal P_r\).  Successive subsequence selection in \([0,1]\), followed by diagonal selection, gives a subsequence, still denoted \((n_k)\), for which
\[
 \ell(C)=\lim_{k\to\infty}P\{U_{n_k}\in C\}
\tag{1}
\]
exists for every partition cell \(C\).  These limits are nonnegative, sum to one on each level, and are consistent under refinement.

Construct the limiting measure directly.  Assign to the unique level-zero cell the interval \([0,1)\).  Recursively partition the interval assigned to a cell \(C\) into half-open subintervals assigned to its children \(C'\), in a fixed order, with lengths \(\ell(C')\).  Consistency makes this possible.  Let \(U_r(u)\) be a fixed representative of the level-\(r\) cell whose assigned interval contains \(u\in[0,1)\).  Outside the countable set of interval endpoints the cells are nested, and their diameters make \((U_r(u))_r\) Cauchy.  Compactness gives a limit \(U(u)\in\mathcal K_{a,b}\).  Define \(U\) arbitrarily at the endpoints.  Each \(U_r\) is Borel measurable, so the resulting \(U\) is Borel measurable.  Let \(\mu\) be the pushforward of Lebesgue probability on \([0,1)\) by \(U\).

For continuous \(f:\mathcal K_{a,b}\to\mathbb R\), compactness makes \(f\) uniformly continuous.  Write
\[
 \omega_f(h)=\sup\{|f(u)-f(v)|:u,v\in\mathcal K_{a,b},\
 \|u-v\|_2\le h\},\qquad \omega_f(h)\downarrow0.
\tag{2}
\]
For one representative \(u_C\) per cell,
\[
 \left|E[f(U_{n_k})]-\sum_{C\in\mathcal P_r}
 f(u_C)P\{U_{n_k}\in C\}\right|\le\omega_f(2^{-r}).
\tag{3}
\]
By construction, the same inequality holds with \(U\) and the weights \(\ell(C)\).  First let \(k\to\infty\) in the finite sum using (1), and then let \(r\to\infty\) using (2)--(3).  This gives
\[
 E[f(U_{n_k})]\longrightarrow E[f(U)]=\int f(u)\,d\mu(u).
\]
The pushforward construction supports \(\mu\) on \(\mathcal K_{a,b}\), as required.

statements.statement: In the setting of Theorem 3, suppose the limiting covariance law has finite support \(\mu=\sum_{j=1}^r p_j\delta_{W_j}\), where \(r<\infty\), every \(p_j>0\), \(\sum_jp_j=1\), and every \(W_j\) is positive definite. For a fixed nonzero \(c\), the deterministic sandwich \(\Sigma\) has asymptotic coverage \(1-\alpha\) at every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) if and only if \(c^\top W_jc=c^\top\Sigma c\) for every \(j\). The same \(\Sigma\) is valid at every level for every nonzero contrast if and only if \(W_j=\Sigma\) for every \(j\).
statements.proof_tex:
For the finite law in the statement and every Borel set \(D\),
\[
 \mu(D)=\sum_{j=1}^rp_j\mathbf1\{W_j\in D\}.
\tag{1}
\]
Since every \(p_j\) is strictly positive, \(c^\top Vc=c^\top\Sigma c\) holds \(\mu\)-almost surely if and only if \(c^\top W_jc=c^\top\Sigma c\) for every \(j\).  The contrastwise deterministic-sandwich theorem gives the first equivalence.  Likewise, \(V=\Sigma\) holds \(\mu\)-almost surely if and only if \(W_j=\Sigma\) for every \(j\); the matrixwise theorem gives the second equivalence.

statements.statement:
There is a bounded two-arm, one-dimensional adaptive IPW-Z experiment targeting the causal arm-mean contrast \(\theta^*=E[Y_t(1)]-E[Y_t(2)]\), with uniform overlap and nonsingular Jacobian, for which \(T^{-1}\langle S\rangle_T\ge4\) almost surely but the realized-QV score pivot, and hence its feasible IPW-Z counterpart, has a nonstandard noncentered limit. Specifically, at horizons \(T=2n\), the limit is
\[
 L=\mathbf1\{Z>0\}\frac{2Z+4W/\sqrt3}{\sqrt{28/3}}
 +\mathbf1\{Z\le0\}\frac{2Z+2W}{\sqrt8},
\]
where \(Z,W\) are independent \(N(0,1)\) variables, and
\[
 E[L]=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
 \left(\sqrt{\frac3{28}}-\frac1{\sqrt8}\right)\ne0.
\]
Thus a predictable-QV lower floor and realized-to-predictable QV consistency do not suffice for a Gaussian self-normalized pivot when an early score selects the later variance regime.
statements.justification: This explicit two-regime law is the impossibility certificate showing why a predictable-QV floor and realized-QV consistency cannot by themselves justify self-normalized Gaussian inference.
statements.gap: The witness isolates endogenous variance selection: an early score sign selects the later variance, so realized QV estimates the selected scale but cannot erase the selecting score component.
statements.consumer: It prevents adaptive-experiment software from treating a positive realized variance and a growing predictable variance as a sufficient diagnostic for Gaussian Wald inference.
statements.proof_tex:
We construct the experiment on the even horizons \(T=2n\); this suffices for the asserted subsequential obstruction. Let \(K=2\), \(d=1\), \(\Theta=[-1,1]\), let the context be constant, and take the fixed potential outcomes
\[
 Y_t(1)=Y_t(2)=1\qquad(1\le t\le 2n).
\tag{1}
\]
Thus the full-data law is degenerate, so \(W_1,\ldots,W_T\) are independent and identically distributed and the only randomness is the randomized assignment, as required by \(\mathrm{ass:iid\text{-}full\text{-}data}\). Define
\[
 g(1,x,y;\theta)=y-\frac{\theta}{2},
 \qquad
 g(2,x,y;\theta)=-y-\frac{\theta}{2}.
\tag{2}
\]
Then, by the definition of \(M_P\),
\[
 M_P(\theta)=g(1,x,1;\theta)+g(2,x,1;\theta)=-\theta.
\tag{3}
\]
Consequently the unique causal moment root is
\[
 \theta^*=0=E_P[Y_t(1)]-E_P[Y_t(2)],
 \qquad H=M_P'(0)=-1.
\tag{4}
\]
This verifies the claimed causal target and \(\mathrm{ass:jacobian\text{-}nonsingular}\) with \(h_-=1\). Moreover, on \(\Theta\), the score in (2) is bounded by \(3/2\), its first derivative is \(-1/2\), and its second derivative is zero. Thus \(\mathrm{ass:bounded\text{-}score}\) and \(\mathrm{ass:smooth\text{-}z\text{-}map}\) hold, for example with \(B=3/2\), \(D_1=1/2\), and any positive \(D_2\). Equation (3) verifies \(\mathrm{ass:uniform\text{-}root\text{-}separation}\) with \(\kappa(u)=\min\{u,1\}\): for \(0<u\le1\) the relevant infimum equals \(u\), while for \(u>1\) the constraint set is empty and its infimum is \(+\infty\). Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:root\text{-}interior}\) holds with \(s_\Theta=1\), and one may choose any
\[
 0<\rho<\min\{1,1/(16D_2)\},
\]
which obeys the prescribed restriction because \(\varepsilon=1/4\) below and \(h_-=1\). Set the numerical tolerances \(r_T\) and \(\delta_T\) in \(\mathrm{def:ipw\text{-}z\text{-}estimator}\) equal to zero.

Write
\[
 p_t=P(A_t=1\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}).
\]
For \(t\le n\), set \(p_t=1/2\). Once \(S_n\) has been observed, set, for every \(t>n\),
\[
 p_t=
 \begin{cases}
 1/4,&S_n>0,\\
 1/2,&S_n\le0.
 \end{cases}
\tag{5}
\]
The rule (5) is \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\)-measurable. Conditional on that history, draw \(A_t\) using \(p_t\), independently of the fixed potential outcomes. Hence \(\mathrm{ass:sequential\text{-}randomization}\) holds. Both arm probabilities are at least \(1/4\), so \(\mathrm{ass:uniform\text{-}overlap}\) holds with \(\varepsilon=1/4\).

At the root (4), the IPW score is
\[
 \xi_t=
 \frac{\mathbf 1\{A_t=1\}}{p_t}
 -\frac{\mathbf 1\{A_t=2\}}{1-p_t}.
\tag{6}
\]
Sequential randomization gives
\[
 E_P[\xi_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]
 =p_t\frac1{p_t}-(1-p_t)\frac1{1-p_t}=0,
\tag{7}
\]
so \((\xi_t,\mathcal F_t)\) is a martingale-difference sequence. Its conditional second moment is
\[
 v(p_t):=E_P[\xi_t^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]
 =\frac1{p_t}+\frac1{1-p_t}.
\tag{8}
\]
In particular,
\[
 v(1/2)=4,
 \qquad
 v(1/4)=\frac14(4)^2+\frac34\left(-\frac43\right)^2=\frac{16}{3}.
\tag{9}
\]
It follows directly from the definition of predictable quadratic variation that
\[
 \frac1{2n}\langle S\rangle_{2n}
 =
 \begin{cases}
 14/3,&S_n>0,\\
 4,&S_n\le0.
 \end{cases}
\tag{10}
\]
Thus \((2n)^{-1}\langle S\rangle_{2n}\ge4\) on every assignment path.

We next calculate the limiting score law without imposing an exogenous variance regime. On a common product space, generate the first block and, independently of it and of each other, two candidate second blocks having respectively the score laws in (6) for \(p=1/4\) and \(p=1/2\). A bounded centered variable \(U\) with variance \(\sigma^2\) satisfies, for each fixed real \(u\),
\[
 E\!\left[e^{iuU/\sqrt n}\right]
 =1-\frac{u^2\sigma^2}{2n}+O(n^{-3/2}),
\tag{11}
\]
because the third-order Taylor remainder is bounded uniformly by a constant times \(E|U|^3n^{-3/2}\). Multiplying the characteristic functions of the independent summands in each block, and then those of the three independent blocks, gives
\[
 \left(
 \frac{S_n}{\sqrt n},
 \frac{S^{(1/4)}_{2n}-S_n}{\sqrt n},
 \frac{S^{(1/2)}_{2n}-S_n}{\sqrt n}
 \right)
 \ \Longrightarrow\ 
 \left(2Z,\frac4{\sqrt3}W_1,2W_2\right),
\tag{12}
\]
where \(Z,W_1,W_2\) are independent standard normal variables. Indeed, (11) makes the joint characteristic function converge to
\[
 \exp\!\left[-\frac12\left(4u_1^2+\frac{16}{3}u_2^2+4u_3^2\right)\right],
\]
the characteristic function of the vector on the right side of (12).

The branch-selection map is continuous whenever its first coordinate is nonzero, and \(P(Z=0)=0\). Applying it to (12) therefore yields
\[
 \frac{S_{2n}}{\sqrt n}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ 
 \mathbf 1\{Z>0\}\left(2Z+\frac4{\sqrt3}W_1\right)
 +\mathbf 1\{Z\le0\}(2Z+2W_2).
\tag{13}
\]
If
\[
 W=\mathbf 1\{Z>0\}W_1+\mathbf 1\{Z\le0\}W_2,
\]
then \(W\) is standard normal and independent of \(Z\): for bounded measurable \(f,h\), independence of \(Z,W_1,W_2\) gives
\[
 E[f(Z)h(W)]
 =E[f(Z)\mathbf 1\{Z>0\}]E[h(W_1)]
 +E[f(Z)\mathbf 1\{Z\le0\}]E[h(W_2)]
 =E[f(Z)]E[h(W_1)].
\tag{14}
\]

To compare realized and predictable quadratic variation, put
\[
 D_t=\xi_t^2-E_P[\xi_t^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}].
\]
By (6) and the overlap floor, \(|\xi_t|\le4\), so \((D_t,\mathcal F_t)\) is a bounded martingale-difference sequence with \(|D_t|\le16\). Martingale orthogonality consequently gives
\[
 E_P\!\left[\left\{\frac{[S]_{2n}-\langle S\rangle_{2n}}{n}\right\}^2\right]
 =\frac1{n^2}\sum_{t=1}^{2n}E_P[D_t^2]
 \le\frac{512}{n}\longrightarrow0.
\tag{15}
\]
Thus \(n^{-1}([S]_{2n}-\langle S\rangle_{2n})\to_P0\). Combining (10), (13), and (15), and using that both limiting denominators are strictly positive, proves
\[
 \frac{S_{2n}}{\sqrt{[S]_{2n}}}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ 
 L:=\mathbf1\{Z>0\}\frac{2Z+4W/\sqrt3}{\sqrt{28/3}}
 +\mathbf1\{Z\le0\}\frac{2Z+2W}{\sqrt8}.
\tag{16}
\]
The limit is integrable. From (14), the terms containing \(W\) have mean zero conditionally on \(Z\), while
\[
 E[Z\mathbf1\{Z>0\}]=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}},
 \qquad
 E[Z\mathbf1\{Z\le0\}]=-\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 E[L]
 =\frac2{\sqrt{2\pi}}
 \left(\sqrt{\frac3{28}}-\frac1{\sqrt8}\right)\ne0.
\tag{17}
\]
Since a standard normal variable has mean zero, (17) proves that the limit in (16) is not \(N(0,1)\); in particular it is noncentered.

It remains to verify that the feasible estimator and sandwich in the proposition have the same limit. For
\[
 U_t=\frac{\mathbf1\{A_t=1\}}{p_t}
 +\frac{\mathbf1\{A_t=2\}}{1-p_t},
 \qquad R_T=\sum_{t=1}^TU_t,
\]
equations (2) and (6) give the exact affine identity
\[
 G_T(\theta)=\frac1T\left(S_T-\frac\theta2R_T\right).
\tag{18}
\]
Moreover, \(E_P[U_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=2\) and \(0<U_t\le4\). Martingale orthogonality and Chebyshev's inequality therefore imply
\[
 \frac{R_T}{T}\to_P2.
\tag{19}
\]
The same argument applied to the bounded martingale differences \(\xi_t\) gives \(S_T/T\to_P0\). More explicitly, for every \(\zeta>0\),
\[
 P\!\left(\left|\frac{2S_T}{R_T}\right|>\zeta\right)
 \le P(R_T/T<1)+P(2|S_T|/T>\zeta)\longrightarrow0.
\tag{20}
\]
Thus the unique affine root
\[
 \vartheta_T=\frac{2S_T}{R_T}
\tag{21}
\]
belongs to \(\Theta\), and indeed to the \(\rho/2\)-neighborhood of zero, with probability tending to one. On this event the global minimum of \(\|G_T(\theta)\|_2\) over \(\Theta\) is zero. Because the numerical tolerance was set to zero, the preliminary estimator in \(\mathrm{def:ipw\text{-}z\text{-}estimator}\) must equal the unique root \(\vartheta_T\); hence \(\mathcal Z_T=\{\vartheta_T\}\) and the selected local exact root satisfies
\[
 \widehat\theta_T=\vartheta_T
\tag{22}
\]
with probability tending to one. Since \(E_P[S_T^2]=E_P[\langle S\rangle_T]\le(16/3)T\), one has \(S_T/\sqrt T=O_P(1)\). Equations (19), (21), and (22) then yield the exact-root linearization
\[
 \sqrt T\,\widehat\theta_T-\frac{S_T}{\sqrt T}
 =\left(\frac{2T}{R_T}-1\right)\frac{S_T}{\sqrt T}
 \to_P0.
\tag{23}
\]

Differentiating (18) gives
\[
 \widehat H_T=-\frac{R_T}{2T}\to_P-1=H.
\tag{24}
\]
Also, on the event in (22), evaluation at the exact root gives
\[
 \widehat\xi_t=\xi_t-\frac{\widehat\theta_T}{2}U_t.
\tag{25}
\]
Because \(|\xi_t|\le4\), \(U_t\le4\), and \(|\widehat\theta_T|\le1\), (25) implies
\[
 \left|\widehat\Omega_T-\frac{[S]_T}{T}\right|
 \le\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T
 \frac{|\widehat\theta_T|U_t}{2}
 \left(2|\xi_t|+\frac{|\widehat\theta_T|U_t}{2}\right)
 \le20|\widehat\theta_T|
 \to_P0.
\tag{26}
\]
Take \(c=1\), \(h_-=1\), and the constant horizon-specific event-truncation floor \(\omega_{1,T}=4\) in \(\mathrm{def:event\text{-}truncated\text{-}rqv\text{-}sandwich}\). By (24), \(P(\mathcal H_T)\to1\). On \(\mathcal H_T\), (24), (26), and the deterministic bound \([S]_T/T\le16\) imply
\[
 \widehat q_T(1)-\frac{[S]_T}{T}\to_P0.
\tag{27}
\]
Equations (10), (15), and (27) show
\[
 P\{\widehat q_T(1)\ge2\}\longrightarrow1.
\tag{28}
\]
Hence \(P\{\mathcal E_T(1)\}\to1\), and on that event \(\widehat V_T(1)=\widehat q_T(1)\) in dimension one. The denominators in (27) are bounded away from zero with probability tending to one, so (23) and (27) give
\[
 T_T^{\mathrm{rqv}}(1)
 -\frac{S_T}{\sqrt{[S]_T}}
 \to_P0.
\tag{29}
\]
Combining (16) and (29) proves that the feasible IPW--Z pivot has the same nonstandard limit \(L\).

As an exact smallest-instance stress test, take \(n=1\). Enumerating all four assignment paths gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
(A_1,A_2)&P(A_1,A_2)&S_2/\sqrt{[S]_2}&\langle S\rangle_2/2&2S_2/R_2\\ \hline
(1,1)&1/8&3/\sqrt5&14/3&2\\
(1,2)&3/8&1/\sqrt{13}&14/3&2/5\\
(2,1)&1/4&0&4&0\\
(2,2)&1/4&-\sqrt2&4&-2
\end{array}
\tag{30}
\]
The two unconstrained roots outside \(\Theta\) invoke the prescribed fallback; with zero tolerance the four selected estimates are respectively \(1,2/5,0,-1\), whose expectation is \(1/40\ne\theta^*\). Thus no finite-sample unbiasedness is being smuggled into the asymptotic claim. Likewise, at the two-sided critical value \(1\), the exact score-pivot coverage is
\[
 P\!\left\{\left|S_2/\sqrt{[S]_2}\right|\le1\right\}=\frac58
 <2\Phi(1)-1,
\tag{31}
\]
so the smallest instance already fails the corresponding nominal Gaussian coverage. Finally, (10) and (15) simultaneously verify the predictable-QV floor and realized-to-predictable QV consistency. Thus neither property prevents the endogenous selection mechanism in (5), completing the claimed obstruction.

statements.statement:
Let \((X_{n,t},\mathcal G_{n,t})_{t=1}^{N_n}\) be a scalar martingale-difference triangular array, where \(N_n\) and \(h_n\) are deterministic integers satisfying \(0\le h_n<N_n\), and suppose \(|X_{n,t}|\le L<\infty\) almost surely. Let \(\lambda_n\) be a positive \(\mathcal G_{n,h_n}\)-measurable random variable, and let \(\nu_n>0\) be deterministic with \(\lambda_n\ge\nu_n\) almost surely. Define
\[
 S_n=\sum_{t=1}^{N_n}X_{n,t},\qquad
 Q_n=\sum_{t=1}^{N_n}X_{n,t}^2,\qquad
 A_{n,+}^2=\sum_{t=h_n+1}^{N_n}E[X_{n,t}^2\mid\mathcal G_{n,t-1}].
\]
If
\[
 N_n\nu_n\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad
 \frac{h_n}{N_n\nu_n}\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 \frac{A_{n,+}^2}{N_n\lambda_n}\longrightarrow1
 \quad\text{in probability},
\]
then
\[
 \frac{Q_n}{N_n\lambda_n}\longrightarrow1
 \quad\text{in probability},\qquad
 P(Q_n>0)\longrightarrow1,\qquad
 \frac{S_n}{\sqrt{Q_n}}\Rightarrow N(0,1).
\]
All conclusions are uniform over a collection of arrays if \(L\) is common and each displayed convergence premise is uniform over that collection.
statements.proof_tex:
Put \(b_n^2=N_n\lambda_n\).  For \(t>h_n\), define
\[
 Y_{n,t}=X_{n,t}/b_n,\qquad
 v_{n,t}=E[Y_{n,t}^2\mid\mathcal G_{n,t-1}],\qquad
 V_n=\sum_{t=h_n+1}^{N_n}v_{n,t}.
\tag{1}
\]
Division is legal because \(\lambda_n\ge\nu_n>0\).  Since \(b_n\) is \(\mathcal G_{n,h_n}\)-measurable, it is \(\mathcal G_{n,t-1}\)-measurable for \(t>h_n\); hence the suffix is again a martingale-difference array.  The increment bound and the first and third hypotheses give
\[
 \max_{t>h_n}|Y_{n,t}|
 \le\epsilon_n:=\frac{L}{\sqrt{N_n\nu_n}}\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad V_n=\frac{A_{n,+}^2}{N_n\lambda_n}\longrightarrow1
\tag{2}
\]
in probability.

Retain the increment at time \(t>h_n\) only when \(\sum_{s=h_n+1}^{t-1}v_{n,s}\le2\).  This indicator is predictable.  Denote the retained increment and variance by \(\widetilde Y_{n,t}\) and \(\widetilde v_{n,t}\).  Then
\[
 \sum_{t=h_n+1}^{N_n}\widetilde v_{n,t}\le2+\epsilon_n^2.
\tag{3}
\]
For fixed \(u\in\mathbb R\), Taylor's formula and the martingale-difference property imply
\[
 E[e^{iu\widetilde Y_{n,t}}\mid\mathcal G_{n,t-1}]
 =1-\frac{u^2}{2}\widetilde v_{n,t}+r_{n,t},
 \qquad |r_{n,t}|\le\frac{|u|^3}{6}\epsilon_n\widetilde v_{n,t}.
\tag{4}
\]
Define
\[
 Z_{n,j}=\exp\!\left\{iu\sum_{t=h_n+1}^j\widetilde Y_{n,t}
 +\frac{u^2}{2}\sum_{t=h_n+1}^j\widetilde v_{n,t}\right\}.
\tag{5}
\]
Using (4) and \(|e^x-1-x|\le x^2e^x/2\) for \(x\ge0\), conditional expectation gives
\[
 \left|E[Z_{n,j}\mid\mathcal G_{n,j-1}]-Z_{n,j-1}\right|
 \le C_u e^{u^2(2+\epsilon_n^2)/2}
 \left(\epsilon_n\widetilde v_{n,j}+\widetilde v_{n,j}^2\right).
\tag{6}
\]
Since \(\widetilde v_{n,j}\le\epsilon_n^2\), summing (6) and using (3) gives \(E[Z_{n,N_n}]\to1\).  By (2), stopping changes the suffix only on \(\{V_n>2\}\), whose probability tends to zero.  The stopped total variance \(\widetilde V_n=\sum_{t=h_n+1}^{N_n}\widetilde v_{n,t}\) converges in probability to one and is bounded by \(2+\epsilon_n^2\), so
\[
 E\left|1-\exp\{u^2(\widetilde V_n-1)/2\}\right|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{7}
\]
The identity
\[
 e^{-u^2/2}Z_{n,N_n}
 =e^{iu\sum_t\widetilde Y_{n,t}}
 e^{u^2(\widetilde V_n-1)/2}
\]
together with (6)--(7), followed by removal of \(\{V_n>2\}\), shows that the suffix characteristic function converges to \(e^{-u^2/2}\) for every \(u\).  The characteristic-function continuity criterion gives
\[
 \sum_{t=h_n+1}^{N_n}X_{n,t}/b_n\Rightarrow N(0,1).
\tag{8}
\]

The prefix is negligible on this scale.  Martingale orthogonality and boundedness give
\[
 E\left(\sum_{t=1}^{h_n}X_{n,t}\right)^2
 =\sum_{t=1}^{h_n}E[X_{n,t}^2]\le h_nL^2.
\tag{9}
\]
Since \(b_n^2\ge N_n\nu_n\), Chebyshev's inequality and the second hypothesis yield
\[
 b_n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{h_n}X_{n,t}\longrightarrow0
 \quad\text{in probability}.
\tag{10}
\]
Equations (8)--(10) prove \(S_n/b_n\Rightarrow N(0,1)\).

For realized quadratic variation put \(D_{n,t}=Y_{n,t}^2-v_{n,t}\) for \(t>h_n\).  These are martingale differences and
\[
 E[D_{n,t}^2\mid\mathcal G_{n,t-1}]
 \le E[Y_{n,t}^4\mid\mathcal G_{n,t-1}]
 \le\epsilon_n^2v_{n,t}.
\tag{11}
\]
Under the same predictable stopping rule, martingale orthogonality bounds the second moment of the stopped sum by \(\epsilon_n^2(2+\epsilon_n^2)\).  Removing \(\{V_n>2\}\) gives
\[
 \sum_{t=h_n+1}^{N_n}D_{n,t}\longrightarrow0
 \quad\text{in probability}.
\tag{12}
\]
The prefix squares satisfy
\[
 0\le b_n^{-2}\sum_{t=1}^{h_n}X_{n,t}^2
 \le\frac{h_nL^2}{N_n\nu_n}\longrightarrow0.
\tag{13}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \frac{Q_n}{b_n^2}
 =b_n^{-2}\sum_{t=1}^{h_n}X_{n,t}^2+V_n
 +\sum_{t=h_n+1}^{N_n}D_{n,t}
 \longrightarrow1
\tag{14}
\]
in probability.  Hence \(P(Q_n>0)\to1\).  On \(\{Q_n/b_n^2\in[1/2,3/2]\}\), division is legal, and (8)--(10), (14), and continuity of \(x\mapsto x^{-1/2}\) give
\[
 \frac{S_n}{\sqrt{Q_n}}
 =\frac{S_n/b_n}{\sqrt{Q_n/b_n^2}}\Rightarrow N(0,1).
\tag{15}
\]
Every bound depends only on the common \(L\) and the three displayed premise errors.  Applying the argument to any contrary sequence of member arrays proves all asserted uniform conclusions.

sampling_model.design: Known, logged, context-dependent randomization \(\pi_t(a\mid X_t,\mathcal F_{t-1})=\Pi(a\mid X_t,\eta_{t-1})\) updated by a history-measurable recursion.
sampling_model.units: A growing sequence of independent full-data decision occasions \(W_t\); the inferential dependence is induced by the common adaptive policy state.
sampling_model.treatment: A finite action set with sequential randomization and consistency \(Y_t=Y_t(A_t)\).
sampling_model.overlap: Known clipping floor \(\pi_t(a\mid X_t,\mathcal F_{t-1})\ge\varepsilon\), common over the triangular-array law class.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: No outcome-model nuisance is required for identification; a preliminary moment-norm minimizer localizes a total measurable exact-root selector, the Z-Jacobian and realized score quadratic variation are estimated on the observed adaptive path, and the sandwich is set to \(I_d\) off the common invertibility event.

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: Saco's Theorem 5.14 gives pointwise realized-QV Studentized inference for a distinct logged-propensity martingale AIPW/DML setup. The present theorem instead proves uniform early-scale conditions, exact-root localization, feasible Jacobian inversion, truncation inactivity, and coverage for bounded adaptive IPW-Z scores. The classes are not known to be nested, and no wholesale transfer or strict tightening is claimed.

Guo and Xu study a different decaying-overlap regime in which Gaussian IPW-Z conclusions require stabilization of scaled inverse propensities. Their numerical two-mode example motivates the basin question but proves neither the present finite-attractor class nor the early-scale projected class.

Shen and coauthors obtain target-specific normal inference under deterministic stability of a target-relevant direction. The present result uses an early-measurable random suffix scale and same-path self-normalization; the regimes and estimators are not known to be nested.
For generalized Gaussian Thompson sampling, a continuous-state SDE invariant law controls optimal-arm pull proportions and nonstandard normalized-mean limits in the multiple-optimum regime.

Leiner, Dunn, and Ramdas study stationary-evaluation-policy off-policy M-estimation with flexible variance stabilization under unstable logging. Their class and target are not established to contain, or be contained in, the present early-scale adaptive IPW-Z class.

Conditional on entering an attraction domain, stochastic approximation locks into a prescribed stable equilibrium with an explicit high-probability bound; this does not by itself supply the present compact-uniform Cesaro modulus or early-scale suffix-QV approximation.

tldr: The field-tier contribution is a conditional finite-attractor theorem bundle for adaptive causal IPW-Z inference. Under common score, derivative, Jacobian-lower-bound, policy, covariance-lower-bound, root-separation, attraction, and local root-search envelopes, with attainable basins defined as the positive-mass support of the tail selector, the bundle derives a basin-stable finite Gaussian mixture with predictable-QV error controlled by \(r_T+\delta_T\), proves that an always-defined same-path realized-QV sandwich is uniformly pivotal and asymptotically untruncated, and gives exact deterministic-sandwich boundaries: every-level validity for one contrast holds if and only if that contrast's variance is basin-invariant, while validity for all contrasts holds if and only if the full covariance is deterministic. Theorem 2 has one direct strict-tightening comparator, Saco's pointwise realized-QV result; the remaining named papers provide motivation, ingredients, or orthogonal regimes rather than a second strict frontier. An elementary bounded two-basin law verifies that contrastwise invariance need not imply matrix invariance. The slope-projected limit set of the augmented bounded Guo--Xu Markov chain remains an open dynamics question with no class-membership or inference claim.

project_justification.gap: Saco supplies the one direct pointwise realized-QV comparator, but not uniform verification over an endogenous finite-attractor class. Guo--Xu and Shen and coauthors supply adjacent stable-policy and directional-stability results, Han studies continuous SDE-invariant Thompson-sampling pull proportions and raw-arm-mean inference, and Leiner, Dunn, and Ramdas study stationary-evaluation-policy off-policy M-estimation with flexible variance stabilization under unstable logging. Zhang, Janson, and Murphy instead study pooled longitudinal adaptive sampling with Z-estimation and an adaptive sandwich estimator in a fixed-within-user, growing-participant regime. Existing stochastic-approximation results control lock-in only after entry into an attraction domain, and the Guo--Xu two-mode example remains numerical.
project_justification.niche: The unoccupied field-tier object is a conditional recursion-level uniform limit theory that preserves the random basin, validates a finite-sample-defined same-path studentizer, and states exact contrastwise and matrixwise boundaries for deterministic-sandwich inference. The absence of a second direct strict-tightening comparator caps the positioning at field tier, which is the requested floor and achieved target.
project_justification.fill: The publishable contribution is the conditional finite-attractor theorem bundle: a basin-stable causal IPW-Z finite Gaussian mixture, a uniformly feasible same-path realized-QV pivot, and exact contrastwise and matrixwise deterministic-sandwich boundaries. A finite-attractor class indexed by common score, derivative, Jacobian lower, policy, covariance lower, root-separation, attraction, and local root-search envelopes converts policy dynamics into predictable-QV control with error \(r_T+\delta_T\); its attainable-basin index set is the positive-mass support of the tail selector. The score and derivative envelopes already imply \(\Omega_j\preceq(KB^2/\varepsilon)I_d\) and \(\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le KD_1\), so no primitive upper matrix bounds are imposed. The proposal-specific envelope \(e_T=T^{-1/2}+r_T+\delta_T\) combines sampling, attraction, and approximation errors. A preliminary moment-norm minimizer localizes a compact empirical-root set; martingale concentration and a quantitative inverse-function argument make the exact-root selector active with probability tending uniformly to one. Stable martingale convergence supplies the mixture, event-truncated realized QV supplies the feasible pivot, finite normal-mixture identification plus polarization supplies the two necessity results, and a bounded in-class law certifies strict logical separation of the directional and matrix frontiers.

related_work: Guo and Xu, Theorems 3.2--3.3, prove marginal and joint IPW-Z Gaussian limits after scaled inverse propensities stabilize; their Section 3.1 no-intercept clipped-LinUCB example supplies numerical evidence of two modes, not a proved finite-attractor theorem or certification of the present class. Guo--Xu is an informed-by comparator. Saco, Theorem 5.14 and Design A in Section 6.6, establishes a pointwise realized-QV pivot under variance growth and illustrates random post-burn-in variance; Theorem 2 is the sole direct strict tightening, giving uniform validity over the conditional finite-attractor class and deriving truncation inactivity from common basin-covariance, attraction, and exact-root localization controls. The Abstract and Introduction of Shen and coauthors distinguish directional stability from full-matrix stability; that distinction informs Theorems 3--4, while the finite-basin every-level converses and bounded separation witness are not presented as a strict comparator chain. Han studies an orthogonal instability mechanism and target: for generalized Gaussian Thompson sampling, Proposition 2.6 and Theorem 2.7 on PDF pages 9--10, together with introduction equation (1.4) on page 4, identify the joint optimal-arm pull-proportion and noise limit with the unique invariant law of a continuous-state SDE. Han's Theorem 3.2 on PDF page 12 and introduction equation (1.5) on page 5 give Gaussian normalized-mean limits for stable arms and an SDE-defined semi-universal limit for multiple optimal arms; the body reports simulation evidence that the latter law is genuinely non-Gaussian, and Corollary 3.3 on PDF page 13 constructs confidence intervals from its quantiles. Han is close motivation, not a result anticipating Theorems 1--4 or the bounded Guo--Xu certification question. Leiner, Dunn, and Ramdas study off-policy M-estimation under working-model misspecification for adaptively collected bandit data. Their target is a projected solution under a stationary evaluation policy, and flexible variance stabilization permits unstable or nonconvergent logging policies; this is an informed-by comparator rather than a same-path-QV or finite-attractor result. Borkar supplies local lock-in bounds, and Pemantle supplies unstable-point avoidance, but neither certifies the bounded recursion. Aldous and Eagleson supply stable-convergence language. Mourrat supplies only the bounded-martingale central-limit and quadratic-variation ingredient. Teicher together with Andrews and Mallows supplies identification of centered normal scale mixtures. Qian and coauthors and Liao and coauthors define the HeartSteps causal-excursion consumer. Zhang, Janson, and Murphy study pooled longitudinal adaptive sampling with Z-estimation and an adaptive sandwich estimator in a fixed-within-user, growing-participant regime. Thus the comparison supports a field-tier conditional theorem bundle, with Saco as its only strict-tightening comparator and no second strict frontier.

honest_scope: The project establishes a field-tier inference frontier conditional on membership in the common-envelope finite-attractor class. Saco is the only direct strict-tightening comparator; the absence of a second direct strict frontier caps the contribution at field tier, which is the requested floor and achieved target. Guo--Xu, Shen and coauthors, Han, Leiner--Dunn--Ramdas, Borkar, and the remaining cited papers serve as informed-by comparators, ingredients, close motivation, or orthogonal regimes. The project treats a growing-horizon superpopulation adaptive experiment with a known randomization rule, not a pure fixed-finite-population randomization theorem. The bounded two-basin construction is solely an elementary, non-novel existence witness for strict logical separation between contrastwise and matrixwise invariance. It is not evidence that either the specified bounded Rademacher analogue or the published Gaussian no-intercept Guo--Xu recursion satisfies the finite-attractor, attraction, or common-envelope conditions. The open-ended question concerns only the slope-projected dynamics of the augmented bounded chain and does not assert membership in \(\mathfrak P_T\) or applicability of Theorems 1--2. Any future inference theorem must separately specify its causal score, parameter space, unique target root, nonzero target contrast, induced scalar target, and every class assumption. The Gaussian moment extension remains optional and open. When \(m=1\), \(J=1\), \(V_J=V_1\) is deterministic, Theorem 1 is ordinary asymptotic normality, Theorem 2 is ordinary realized-QV studentization, and Theorems 3--4 allow \(\Sigma=V_1\).
